meta.title: Add Memory to an Agent
meta.thesis: Add Memory to an Agent is practical when learners can apply it to this concrete case: A ticket assistant needs to remember issue facts across turns while keeping the final answer grounded. By the end, they should be able to build or review memory-enabled agent thin slice with write, retrieve, and reject rules, measure facts reused correctly in follow-up turns, and catch the failure where the agent retrieves an outdated preference and ignores the latest user correction.

mentalMap.title: Add Memory to an Agent: mental map
mentalMap.caption: Build memory by separating thread state, accepted long-term records, scoped retrieval, traceability, and user correction.
mentalMap.oneLineThesis: Adding memory to an agent is a product-state change: implement the smallest explicit memory behavior and test write, recall, and correction.

modules.title: Pick one memory behavior to ship
modules.sub: Do not start with universal remembering.
modules.summary: The first memory feature should be small enough to review.
objectives: State the user-visible behavior memory improves.
Choose one memory type to implement first.

blocks.title: A memory build starts with a behavior, not a database

spans.text: Problem anchor: a coding tutor should remember that a learner prefers TypeScript examples. It should not remember every emotional aside, every code snippet, or facts from retrieved docs.
The first slice accepts explicit preference statements, stores provenance, retrieves them for lesson/example tasks, and lets the learner correct them. That is enough to prove the architecture.
If the feature cannot name a no-write case, it is too broad.

blocks.analogy: Start with one labeled drawer before buying a warehouse.

blocks.title: Worked acceptance card for preference memory

spans.text: Accept: “Remember that I prefer TypeScript examples.” Reject: “I hate recursion today.” Reject: “The docs say pgvector uses HNSW.” The first is durable preference, the second transient mood, the third external knowledge for RAG.
The acceptance card becomes the regression suite seed.

items.text: Define how users edit or delete it.

blocks.title: Scope check
blocks.prompt: Which requirement is best for a first memory slice?

options.text: Remember explicit example-language preferences and retrieve them for lesson tasks.
Store all retrieved documents as user memory.

blocks.explanation: Small typed memory is safer and easier to validate.

modules.title: Separate thread state, facts, and RAG
modules.sub: Memory should not absorb every kind of context.
modules.summary: The build needs boundaries before code.
objectives: Distinguish thread checkpoint from long-term memory.

blocks.title: The memory store is not the whole context system

spans.text: Thread state keeps the current run coherent. Long-term memory personalizes future runs. RAG supplies grounded external facts. The app database stores canonical records. Workflow engines store exact progress.
For the TypeScript preference slice, the memory store only holds user preference records. It does not store lesson content, billing status, or source documents.
Add a routing table before creating tables.

blocks.analogy: Use the right shelf: diary, library, ledger, and task board are different things.

options.name: Current plan/tool results

cells.text: Needed only to resume this run.

options.whenToUse: Use inside one conversation or workflow.

cells.text: Source of truth lives outside user memory.

blocks.title: Routing table
blocks.prompt: Where should product documentation facts go?

options.text: In a RAG or document index, not as inferred user memory.
Only in transient model hidden state.

blocks.explanation: External facts need source provenance and document refresh, not personalization memory.

modules.title: Write accepted memories with provenance
modules.sub: The extractor proposes records that policy can reject.
modules.summary: The write path should make future correction possible.

blocks.title: Accepted memory is a typed record

spans.text: A minimal memory row can include namespace, type, value, source turn ID, created time, confidence, status, and optional expiration. This is enough to retrieve and correct later.
Avoid opaque transcript dumps. They are hard to inspect, hard to delete selectively, and likely to include sensitive or irrelevant content.
The memory value should be short enough that a user can approve or correct it.

blocks.analogy: A memory row should look like a clean contact card, not a shoebox of receipts.

blocks.title: Case study: write path for language preference

spans.text: The user says, “Please remember: I prefer TypeScript examples.” The extractor proposes `{type: preference, value: prefers TypeScript examples}`. Policy accepts because it is explicit, future-useful, and low sensitivity.
The source turn ID is stored so the UI can later show where the memory came from.

items.text: Create a candidate with type and value.

blocks.title: Write record
blocks.prompt: What field makes later correction explainable?

options.text: The source turn or event that produced the memory.
The CSS class of the chat bubble.

blocks.explanation: Users and operators need to know why a memory exists.

modules.title: Retrieve and inject memories narrowly
modules.sub: Recall should be task-relevant and visible in traces.
modules.summary: Memory retrieval is part of prompt assembly.
objectives: Retrieve only active memories for the current user.
Trace which memory influenced the answer.

blocks.title: Prompt injection of memory should be labeled and minimal

spans.text: When assembling the prompt, include relevant memories under a label such as “User preferences from memory.” Do not let memory masquerade as system policy or external evidence.
Spaced recall: from agent memory, current user instruction and safety policy outrank older memory. Retrieval should be narrow enough that this ordering remains readable.
Every memory in the prompt should appear in the trace with ID and reason.

blocks.title: End-to-end preference memory slice
blocks.explanation: The slice accepts an explicit preference and recalls it only for lesson/example tasks.

predictThenReveal.prompt: Before reading the answer, predict whether the invoice task receives the preference.
predictThenReveal.answer: It does not. The preference is relevant to examples or lessons, not invoice checking.

blocks.title: Recall injection
blocks.prompt: How should a preference memory appear in the model prompt?

options.text: As labeled user preference context with provenance, not as system policy or factual evidence.
As a citation to product docs.

blocks.explanation: Memory should influence behavior without pretending to be policy or source truth.

modules.title: Add correction and regression tests
modules.sub: Memory bugs should be caught before they persist.
modules.summary: A memory feature ships with lifecycle tests.
objectives: Create tests for accepted and rejected memories.

blocks.title: The memory test suite protects future sessions

spans.text: Tests should cover explicit remember, transient no-write, sensitive no-write, user namespace isolation, task-relevant recall, correction, deletion, and current-instruction override.
Traces should show memory write candidates, acceptance policy result, stored memory ID, recall query, and prompt injection reason. This makes reviews and incidents diagnosable.
Include one test where the user corrects a false memory and the next run stops using it.

blocks.title: Verify AI output after adding memory

spans.text: Review memory behavior across multiple turns.

items.text: The agent stores only explicit, allowed memory types.
Rejected transient or sensitive content does not appear later.
Recall is scoped to user/workspace, task, status, and memory type.
Users can inspect, correct, delete, or override stored memories.
Tests cover write, no-write, recall, leakage, correction, and deletion cases.

blocks.title: Memory release gate

options.text: A snapshot of the final prose for one user only.
A recall test that stores memory for user A and verifies user B never receives it.

blocks.explanation: Namespace isolation must be tested directly.

questions.q: What is the smallest memory behavior that improves the agent and can be validated end to end?
questions.why: A memory feature is risky if it stores too much before proving consent, provenance, and retrieval scope.
opts: No memory; use RAG or database
questions.rot: Start with one typed memory class, explicit acceptance policy, and tests for no-write and correction cases.
